questions.topic: Adjoint and Determinant of a Matrix
questions.question_text: Let $A$ be a matrix of order $3 \times 3$ and $|A| = 5$. If $|2\,\text{adj}(3A\,\text{adj}(2A))| = 2^{\alpha} \cdot 3^{\beta} \cdot 5^{\gamma}$, $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
We need to compute $|2\,\text{adj}(3A\,\text{adj}(2A))|$.

Step 1: For an $n \times n$ matrix, $|\text{adj}(M)| = |M|^{n-1}$ and $|kM| = k^n|M|$.

Here $n=3$, $|A|=5$.

Step 2: Compute $|2A| = 2^3|A| = 8 \times 5 = 40$.

Step 3: $\text{adj}(2A)$ has determinant $|2A|^{n-1} = 40^2 = 1600$.

Step 4: $3A\,\text{adj}(2A)$ — compute its determinant:
$|3A \cdot \text{adj}(2A)| = |3A| \cdot |\text{adj}(2A)| = 3^3 \cdot 5 \cdot (2^3 \cdot 5)^2 = 27 \cdot 5 \cdot 64 \cdot 25 = 27 \cdot 3^6 \cdot |A|^2 \cdot ...$

Let me redo systematically:
$|2\,\text{adj}(3A\,\text{adj}(2A))|$
$= 2^3 \cdot |\text{adj}(3A\,\text{adj}(2A))|$
$= 2^3 \cdot |3A\,\text{adj}(2A)|^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot (|3A| \cdot |\text{adj}(2A)|)^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot (3^3|A| \cdot |2A|^2)^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot (3^3 \cdot 5 \cdot (2^3 \cdot 5)^2)^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot (3^3 \cdot 5 \cdot 2^6 \cdot 5^2)^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot (3^3 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 2^6)^2$
$= 2^3 \cdot 3^6 \cdot 5^6 \cdot 2^{12}$
$= 2^{15} \cdot 3^6 \cdot 5^6$

So $\alpha = 15$, $\beta = 6$, $\gamma = 6$.
$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 27$.

questions.question_text: Let a line passing through the point $(4,1,0)$ intersect the line $L_1: \dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y-2}{3} = \dfrac{z-3}{4}$ at the point $A(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ and the line $L_2: x-6 = y = -z+4$ at the point $B(a,b,c)$. Then $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \alpha & \beta & \gamma \\ a & b & c \end{vmatrix}$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Let $A = (2p+1, 3p+2, 4p+3)$ be a point on $L_1$ and $B = (q+6, q, 4-q)$ be a point on $L_2$.

The line $PA$ (where $P=(4,1,0)$) has direction ratios: $(2p-3, 3p+1, 4p+3)$.
The line $PB$ has direction ratios: $(q+2, q-1, 4-q)$.

Since $P$, $A$, $B$ are collinear (all on the same line through $P$):
$\dfrac{2p-3}{q+2} = \dfrac{3p+1}{q-1} = \dfrac{4p+3}{4-q}$

From the first two ratios: $(2p-3)(q-1) = (3p+1)(q+2)$
$\Rightarrow pq - 2p - 3q + 3 = 3pq + 6p + q + 2$
$\Rightarrow pq + rp + 4q - 1 = 0$ ...(1)

From ratios 2 and 3: $(3p+1)(4-q) = (4p+3)(q-1)$
$12p - 3pq + 4 - q = 4pq - 4p + 3q - 3$
$7pq - 16p + 4q - 7 = 0$ ...(2)

Also from equations: $8p - 2pq - 12 + 3q = 4pq + 8p + 3q + 6$
$6pq = -18 \Rightarrow pq = -3$.

Solving: $8p + 4q = 4 \Rightarrow 2p + q = 1$ and $-21 - 16p + 4q - 7 = 0 \Rightarrow 4p - q = -7$.
Adding: $6p = -6 \Rightarrow p = -1$, $q = 3$.

$A(-1,-1,-1)$, $B(9,3,1)$.

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1(-1+9) - 0 + 1(-3+9) = ... $

Expanding along row 1: $1 \cdot |{-1,-1;3,1}| - 0 + 1 \cdot |{-1,-1;9,3}|$
$= 1(-1+3) + 1(-3+9) = 2 + 6 = 8$.

questions.question_text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^2 + \sqrt{3}x - 16 = 0$, and $\gamma$ and $\delta$ be the roots of $x^2 + 3x - 1 = 0$. If $P_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n$ and $Q_n = \gamma^n + \delta^n$, then $\dfrac{P_{25} + \sqrt{3}P_{24}}{2P_{23}} + \dfrac{Q_{25} - Q_{23}}{Q_{24}}$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots of $x^2 + \sqrt{3}x - 16 = 0$, we have $P_n + \sqrt{3}P_{n-1} - 16P_{n-2} = 0$.

So $P_{25} + \sqrt{3}P_{24} = 16P_{23}$.
$\dfrac{P_{25} + \sqrt{3}P_{24}}{2P_{23}} = \dfrac{16P_{23}}{2P_{23}} = 8$.

Since $\gamma, \delta$ are roots of $x^2 + 3x - 1 = 0$, we have $Q_n + 3Q_{n-1} - Q_{n-2} = 0$.

$Q_{25} - Q_{23} = \gamma^{25} + \delta^{25} - \gamma^{23} - \delta^{23}$
$= \gamma^{23}(\gamma^2 - 1) + \delta^{23}(\delta^2 - 1)$
$= \gamma^{23}(-3\gamma) + \delta^{23}(-3\delta)$ (using $\gamma^2 = 1 - 3\gamma$... wait: $\gamma^2 + 3\gamma - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \gamma^2 - 1 = -3\gamma$)
$= -3(\gamma^{24} + \delta^{24}) = -3Q_{24}$.

So $\dfrac{Q_{25} - Q_{23}}{Q_{24}} = -3$.

Answer: $8 + (-3) = 5$.

questions.topic: Relations – Counting Elements and Reflexive Closure
questions.question_text: Let $A = \{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A$ defined by $xRy$ if and only if $0 \le x^2 + 2y \le 4$. Let $\ell$ be the number of elements in $R$ and $m$ be the minimum number of elements required to be added in $R$ to make it a reflexive relation. Then $\ell + m$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
The condition is $0 \le x^2 + 2y \le 4$, i.e. $-x^2/2 \le y \le (4-x^2)/2$, i.e. $-2y \le x^2 \le 4-2y$.

For each $y \in A$, find valid $x$ values:
$y=-3$: $0 \le x^2 + 2(-3) \le 4 \Rightarrow 6 \le x^2 \le 10 \Rightarrow x \in \{-3,3\}$
$y=-2$: $0 \le x^2-4 \le 4 \Rightarrow 4 \le x^2 \le 8 \Rightarrow x \in \{-2,2\}$
$y=-1$: $0 \le x^2-2 \le 4 \Rightarrow 2 \le x^2 \le 6 \Rightarrow x \in \{-2,2\}$
$y=0$: $0 \le x^2 \le 4 \Rightarrow x \in \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$
$y=1$: $0 \le x^2+2 \le 4 \Rightarrow -2 \le x^2 \le 2 \Rightarrow x \in \{-1,0,1\}$
$y=2$: $0 \le x^2+4 \le 4 \Rightarrow -4 \le x^2 \le 0 \Rightarrow x \in \{0\}$
$y=3$: $0 \le x^2+6 \le 4 \Rightarrow$ no solution.

So $\ell = 2+2+2+5+3+1+0 = 15$.

For reflexivity, we need $(a,a) \in R$ for all $a \in A$. Check diagonal pairs in $R$:
$(0,0)$: $y=0, x=0$ ✓ (included)
$(-1,-1)$: $0 \le 1-2 = -1$: NOT in $R$
$(1,1)$: $0 \le 1+2=3 \le 4$ ✓
$(-2,-2)$: $0 \le 4-4=0 \le 4$ ✓
$(2,2)$: $0 \le 4+4=8$: NOT ≤4, NOT in $R$
$(-3,-3)$: $0 \le 9-6=3 \le 4$ ✓
$(3,3)$: $0 \le 9+6=15$: NOT in $R$

Missing: $(-1,-1), (2,2), (3,3)$, so $m=3$.
$\ell + m = 15+3 = 18$.

questions.question_text: A line passing through the point $P(\sqrt{5}, \sqrt{5})$ intersects the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{36} + \dfrac{y^2}{25} = 1$ at $A$ and $B$ such that $(PA)\cdot(PB)$ is maximum. Then $5(PA^2 + PB^2)$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Parametrize line through $P(\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5})$ as $Q = (\sqrt{5}+r\cos\theta, \sqrt{5}+r\sin\theta)$.

Substituting into ellipse: $25(\sqrt{5}+r\cos\theta)^2 + 36(\sqrt{5}+r\sin\theta)^2 = 900$.

Expanding: $r^2(25\cos^2\theta+36\sin^2\theta) + 2\sqrt{5}r(25\cos\theta+36\sin\theta) + 25\cdot5+36\cdot5 - 900 = 0$
$r^2(25+11\sin^2\theta) + 2\sqrt{5}r(25\cos\theta+36\sin\theta) - 595 = 0$.

$PA \cdot PB = |r_1 r_2| = \dfrac{595}{25+11\sin^2\theta}$, which is maximum when $\sin^2\theta = 0$, i.e. line parallel to x-axis.

Line: $y = \sqrt{5}$. Substituting in ellipse: $\dfrac{x^2}{36} + \dfrac{1}{5} = 1 \Rightarrow x^2 = 36 \cdot \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{144}{5}$.

$A = (\sqrt{5} - \frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}, \sqrt{5})$, $B = (\sqrt{5} + \frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}, \sqrt{5})$.

$PA^2 = (\sqrt{5} - \frac{12}{\sqrt{5}} - \sqrt{5})^2 = \frac{144}{5}$
$PB^2 = \frac{144}{5}$

$PA^2 + PB^2 = 2(5 + \frac{144}{5}) = \frac{338}{5}$.
$5(PA^2+PB^2) = 338$.

questions.question_text: The sum $1 + 3 + 11 + 25 + 45 + 71 + \ldots$ upto 20 terms, is equal to
questions.solution_text:
First order differences: $2, 8, 14, 20, 26, \ldots$ (AP with common difference 6).

Assume $T_n = an^2 + bn + c$.
$T_1 = a+b+c = 1$, $T_2 = 4a+2b+c = 3$, $T_3 = 9a+3b+c = 11$.

From 2nd - 1st: $3a+b = 2$. From 3rd - 2nd: $5a+b = 8$. Subtracting: $2a = 6 \Rightarrow a = 3$.
$b = 2-9 = -7$, $c = 1-3+7 = 5$.

$T_n = 3n^2 - 7n + 5$.

$S_{20} = 3\sum_{n=1}^{20} n^2 - 7\sum_{n=1}^{20} n + 5 \times 20$
$= 3 \cdot \frac{20 \cdot 21 \cdot 41}{6} - 7 \cdot \frac{20 \cdot 21}{2} + 100$
$= 3 \cdot 2870 - 7 \cdot 210 + 100$
$= 8610 - 1470 + 100 = 7240$.

questions.question_text: If the domain of the function $f(x) = \log_e\left(\dfrac{2x-3}{5+4x}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4+3x}{2-x}\right)$ is $[\alpha, \beta)$, then $\alpha^2 + 4\beta$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Conditions: (1) $\dfrac{2x-3}{5+4x} > 0$ and (2) $\left|\dfrac{4+3x}{2-x}\right| \le 1$.

Condition 1: $\dfrac{2x-3}{5+4x} > 0 \Rightarrow x \in \left(-\infty, -\frac{5}{4}\right) \cup \left[\frac{3}{2}, \infty\right)$.

Condition 2: $-1 \le \dfrac{4+3x}{2-x} \le 1$.

Left inequality: $\dfrac{4+3x}{2-x} \ge -1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{4+3x}{2-x} + 1 \ge 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{6+2x}{2-x} \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \in [-3, 2)$.

Right inequality: $\dfrac{4+3x}{2-x} \le 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{4+3x}{2-x} - 1 \le 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{2+4x}{2-x} \le 0 \Rightarrow x \in \left(-\infty, -\frac{1}{2}\right] \cup (2, \infty)$.

Intersection of condition 2: $x \in \left[-3, -\frac{1}{2}\right]$.

Intersection of conditions 1 and 2: $x \in \left[-3, -\frac{5}{4}\right)$.

Wait, also $x \ne 2$ (denominator). So domain = $\left[-3, -\frac{5}{4}\right)$.

$\alpha = -3$, $\beta = -\frac{5}{4}$.
$\alpha^2 + 4\beta = 9 + 4(-\frac{5}{4}) = 9 - 5 = 4$.

questions.question_text: If $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{9}\left(\dfrac{r+3}{2^r}\right)\cdot{}^9C_r = \alpha\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^9 - \beta$, $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(\alpha+\beta)^2$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
$\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^9 \frac{r+3}{2^r} \cdot {}^9C_r = \sum_{r=1}^9 \frac{r}{2^r}{}^9C_r + 3\sum_{r=1}^9 \frac{{}^9C_r}{2^r}$

Using ${}^9C_r \cdot r = 9 \cdot {}^8C_{r-1}$:
$\sum_{r=1}^9 \frac{r}{2^r}{}^9C_r = \frac{9}{2}\sum_{r=1}^9 {}^8C_{r-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{r-1} = \frac{9}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right)^8 = \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^8$

$3\sum_{r=1}^9 \frac{{}^9C_r}{2^r} = 3\left(\sum_{r=0}^9 {}^9C_r\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^r - 1\right) = 3\left(\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right)^9 - 1\right) = 3\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^9 - 3$

Total $= \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^8 + 3\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^9 - 3 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^8 \cdot \left(\frac{9}{2} + \frac{9}{2}\right) - 3 = 9\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^8 \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{2} ...$

Simplifying: $= \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^8 + 3\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^9 - 3 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^9\left(\frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3} + 3\right) - 3 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^9 \cdot 6 - 3$.

So $\alpha = 6$, $\beta = 3$, $(\alpha+\beta)^2 = 81$.

questions.solution_text:
Rewrite as $\tan x = \dfrac{\pi - 2x}{3}$.

Plot $y = \tan x$ and $y = \dfrac{\pi - 2x}{3}$ (a line with slope $-2/3$, y-intercept $\pi/3$) over $x \in [-2\pi, 2\pi]$.

The line passes through $(\pi/2, 0)$ and has slope $-2/3$.

In each period of $\tan x$ (except where excluded), the line can intersect at most once. Counting intersections in the 5 available branches of $\tan x$ on $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ gives 5 solutions.

questions.solution_text:
Apply column operation $C_3 \to C_3 - C_1$:
$y(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x & \cos x & 1+\cos x \\ 27 & 28 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along $C_3$: $y(x) = (1+\cos x) \cdot (27 - 28) \cdot (-1)^{1+3}$... let me expand properly.

Expanding along column 3: $(1+\cos x)\begin{vmatrix}27&28\\1&1\end{vmatrix}\cdot(-1)^{1+3}$
$= (1+\cos x)(27-28)(1) = -(1+\cos x)$.

So $y = -(1+\cos x)$.
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin x$.
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \cos x$.
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + y = \cos x - 1 - \cos x = -1$.

questions.topic: Linear First-Order ODE with Integral Condition
questions.question_text: Let $g$ be a differentiable function such that $\displaystyle\int_0^x g(t)\,dt = x - \int_0^x tg(t)\,dt$, $x \ge 0$ and let $y = y(x)$ satisfy the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y\tan x = 2(x+1)\sec x\, g(x)$, $x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. If $y(0) = 0$, then $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Differentiate $\int_0^x g(t)dt = x - \int_0^x tg(t)dt$ w.r.t. $x$:
$g(x) = 1 - xg(x) \Rightarrow g(x)(1+x) = 1 \Rightarrow g(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+x}$.

ODE: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y\tan x = 2(x+1)\sec x \cdot \dfrac{1}{1+x} = 2\sec x$.

Integrating factor: $e^{-\int \tan x\,dx} = e^{\ln\cos x} = \cos x$.

Multiply: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\cos x) = 2\sec x \cdot \cos x = 2$.

$y\cos x = 2x + C$. Since $y(0)=0$: $C = 0$.
$y = \dfrac{2x}{\cos x} = 2x\sec x$.

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3} \cdot \sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \cdot 2 = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

questions.question_text: A line passes through the origin and makes equal angles with the positive coordinate axes. It intersects the lines $L_1: 2x + y + 6 = 0$ and $L_2: 4x + 2y - p = 0$, $p > 0$, at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. If $AB = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt{2}}$ and the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A$ on the line $L_2$ is $M$, then $\dfrac{AM}{BM}$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Line through origin making equal angles with positive axes: $y = x$ (slope 1).

Intersection with $L_1$: $2x+x+6=0 \Rightarrow x=-2$, so $A=(-2,-2)$.
Intersection with $L_2$: $4x+2x=p \Rightarrow x=p/6$, so $B=(p/6, p/6)$.

$AB = \sqrt{2}|p/6 - (-2)| = \sqrt{2} \cdot |p/6+2| = \frac{9}{\sqrt{2}}$.
$|p/6+2| = 9/2 \Rightarrow p/6 = 5/2 \Rightarrow p = 15$.

So $B=(5/2, 5/2)$.

For foot $M$ of perpendicular from $A=(-2,-2)$ to $L_2: 4x+2y-15=0$ (or $2x+y=15/2$):
$L_2$ has slope $-2$. Perpendicular from $A$ has slope $1/2$.

$\tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is angle between line $y=x$ (slope 1) and $L_2$ (slope $-2$):
$\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{1-(-2)}{1+1\cdot(-2)}\right| = \left|\dfrac{3}{-1}\right| = 3$.

$\dfrac{AM}{BM} = \tan\theta = 3$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $t = 3-x^2 \Rightarrow dt = -2x\,dx \Rightarrow x\,dx = -dt/2$, $x^2 = 3-t$.

$f(x) = \int x^2 \cdot \sqrt{t} \cdot x\,dx = \int (3-t)\sqrt{t}\cdot\left(-\frac{dt}{2}\right)$
$= -\frac{1}{2}\int(3t^{1/2}-t^{3/2})dt = -\frac{1}{2}\left(2t^{3/2} - \frac{2t^{5/2}}{5}\right)+C$
$= -t^{3/2} + \frac{t^{5/2}}{5} + C = \frac{(3-x^2)^{5/2}}{5} - (3-x^2)^{3/2} + C$.

$5f(\sqrt{2}) = 5\left[\frac{1^{5/2}}{5} - 1^{3/2} + C\right] = 1-5+5C = -4 \Rightarrow 5C-4 = -4 \Rightarrow C=0$.

$f(1) = \frac{2^{5/2}}{5} - 2^{3/2} = 2^{1/2}\left(\frac{4}{5}-2\right) = \sqrt{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{6}{5}\right) = -\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{5}$.

questions.question_text: Let the domain of the function $f(x) = \log_2 \log_4 \log_6(3 + 4x - x^2)$ be $(a, b)$. If $\displaystyle\int_0^{b-a} [x^2]\,dx = p - \sqrt{q} - \sqrt{r}$, $p, q, r \in \mathbb{N}$, $\gcd(p,q,r) = 1$, where $[\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function, then $p + q + r$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
For the domain: need $\log_4\log_6(3+4x-x^2) > 0$
$\Rightarrow \log_6(3+4x-x^2) > 1$
$\Rightarrow 3+4x-x^2 > 6$
$\Rightarrow x^2-4x+3 < 0 \Rightarrow (x-1)(x-3)<0 \Rightarrow x \in (1,3)$.

So $a=1$, $b=3$, $b-a=2$.

$\int_0^2 [x^2]\,dx = \int_0^1 0\,dx + \int_1^{\sqrt{2}} 1\,dx + \int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} 2\,dx + \int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2} 3\,dx$
$= 0 + (\sqrt{2}-1) + 2(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}) + 3(2-\sqrt{3})$
$= \sqrt{2}-1+2\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{2}+6-3\sqrt{3}$
$= 5 - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$.

So $p=5, q=2, r=3$, $\gcd(5,2,3)=1$.
$p+q+r = 10$.

questions.question_text: The radius of the smallest circle which touches the parabolas $y = x^2 + 2$ and $x = y^2 + 2$ is
questions.solution_text:
Both parabolas are symmetric about $y=x$. The smallest circle touching both will have center on $y=x$.

For $y=x^2+2$: $dy/dx = 2x = 1 \Rightarrow x=1/2, y=9/4$. Point $B=(1/2, 9/4)$.
For $x=y^2+2$: by symmetry, point $A=(9/4, 1/2)$.

$AB = \sqrt{(9/4-1/2)^2+(1/2-9/4)^2} = \sqrt{2(7/4)^2} = \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{4}$.

Radius $= AB/2 = \dfrac{7\sqrt{2}}{8}$.

questions.solution_text:
$f(0^-) = \lim_{x\to 0^-}(1+ax)^{1/x} = e^a$.

$f(0) = 1+b$.

For $f(0^+)$: as $x \to 0^+$: $\dfrac{(x+4)^{1/2}-2}{(x+c)^{1/3}-2}$.
For this to be finite and nonzero, need $c^{1/3} = 2 \Rightarrow c = 8$.

Using L'Hôpital or Taylor expansion as $x \to 0$:
$\frac{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+4}}}{\frac{1}{3}(x+c)^{-2/3}} \bigg|_{x=0} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{3}\cdot c^{-2/3}} = \frac{3c^{2/3}}{4} = \frac{3 \cdot 4}{4} = 3$.

For continuity: $e^a = 1+b = 3$.
$e^a = 3$, $b = 2$, $c = 8$.
$e^a \cdot bc = 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 8 = 48$.

questions.question_text: Line $L_1$ passes through the point $(1, 2, 3)$ and is parallel to $z$-axis. Line $L_2$ passes through the point $(\lambda, 5, 6)$ and is parallel to $y$-axis. Let for $\lambda = \lambda_1, \lambda_2$, $\lambda_2 < \lambda_1$, the shortest distance between the two lines be 3. Then the square of the distance of the point $(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, 7)$ from the line $L_1$ is
questions.solution_text:
$L_1: \dfrac{x-1}{0} = \dfrac{y-2}{0} = \dfrac{z-3}{1}$ (parallel to z-axis).
$L_2: \dfrac{x-\lambda}{0} = \dfrac{y-5}{1} = \dfrac{z-6}{0}$ (parallel to y-axis).

Shortest distance $= |\lambda - 1| = 3 \Rightarrow \lambda = 4$ or $\lambda = -2$.
$\lambda_1 = 4, \lambda_2 = -2$.

Distance from $(4, -2, 7)$ to $L_1$ (which passes through $(1,2,3)$ parallel to z-axis):
$L_1$ consists of points $(1, 2, t)$. Foot of perpendicular: $t = 7$, foot = $(1,2,7)$.
$\text{dist}^2 = (4-1)^2 + (-2-2)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$.

questions.question_text: All five letter words are made using all the letters A, B, C, D, E and arranged as in an English dictionary with serial numbers. Let the word at serial number $n$ be denoted by $W_n$. Let the probability $P(W_n)$ of choosing the word $W_n$ satisfy $P(W_n) = 2P(W_{n-1})$, $n > 1$. If $P(\text{CDBEA}) = \dfrac{2^\alpha}{2^\beta - 1}$, $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha + \beta$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
Let $P(W_1) = x$. Since $P(W_n) = 2P(W_{n-1})$, probabilities form a GP: $x, 2x, 4x, \ldots, 2^{119}x$.
$\sum_{i=1}^{120} P(W_i) = 1 \Rightarrow x(2^{120}-1) = 1 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{2^{120}-1}$.

Find the serial number of CDBEA:
Words starting with A: $4! = 24$
Words starting with B: $4! = 24$
Words starting with CA: $3! = 6$
Words starting with CB: $3! = 6$
Words starting with CDA: $2! = 2$
Words starting with CDB: $2! = 2$ — wait: CDBAE=1, CDBEA=2 (after CDBAE)

Wait: After CDA__, CDB__:
CDBAE, CDBAE=1, CDBEA=2 → order within CDB: AE comes before EA.
Serial = 24+24+6+6+2+2 = 64. So $n = 64$.

$P(W_{64}) = 2^{63} x = \dfrac{2^{63}}{2^{120}-1}$.

So $\alpha = 63$, $\beta = 120$, $\alpha+\beta = 183$.

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, $\vec{c} = \lambda\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ and $\hat{d}$ be a unit vector such that $\vec{a}\times\hat{d} = \vec{b}\times\hat{d}$ and $\vec{c}\cdot\hat{d} = 1$. If $\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$, then $|3\lambda\hat{d}+\mu\vec{c}|^2$ is equal to
questions.solution_text:
$\vec{a}\times\hat{d} = \vec{b}\times\hat{d} \Rightarrow (\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\hat{d} = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{d} \parallel (\vec{a}-\vec{b})$.
$\vec{a}-\vec{b} = -2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}| = 3$.
$\hat{d} = t(-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$, $|\hat{d}|=1 \Rightarrow |t|=1/3$.

$\vec{c} \perp \vec{a}$: $(0)\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$: $0+\lambda+\mu = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = -\lambda$.
$\vec{c} = \lambda(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$, $|\vec{c}|^2 = 2\lambda^2$.

$\vec{c}\cdot\hat{d} = 1$: $\lambda\hat{j}-\lambda\hat{k}) \cdot t(-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) = t(-\lambda-2\lambda) = -3\lambda t = 1$.
$\lambda t = -1/3$.

With $t = 1/3$: $\lambda = -1$, $\mu = 1$. $\lambda^2 = 1$.
$\hat{d} = \frac{1}{3}(-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$.

$|3\lambda\hat{d}+\mu\vec{c}|^2 = 9\lambda^2|\hat{d}|^2 + \mu^2|\vec{c}|^2 + 6\lambda\mu(\hat{d}\cdot\vec{c})$
$= 9(1)(1) + (1)(2) + 6(-1)(1)(1)$... wait $\hat{d}\cdot\vec{c} = 1$.
$= 9 - 2 \cdot 2\lambda^2... $

Let me directly: $3\lambda = -3$, so $3\lambda\hat{d} = -3 \cdot \frac{1}{3}(-2,-1,2) = (2,1,-2)$.
$\mu\vec{c} = 1\cdot(-1)(0,1,-1) = (0,-1,1)$.
Sum: $(2, 0, -1)$, $|\text{sum}|^2 = 4+0+1 = 5$.

Numbers with even digit sum = $4500000 = 9 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^5 = 9.5 \times 10^5$.

questions.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics – Melting of Ice
questions.question_text:
During the melting of a slab of ice at 273 K at atmospheric pressure:
(1) Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
(2) Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
(3) Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
(4) Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.

options.text: Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.

questions.solution_text:
Ice has greater volume than water at the same mass. So when ice melts, volume decreases. Since the system contracts against atmospheric pressure, the atmosphere does positive work on the system ($W$ done on system is positive, i.e. $W$ done by system is negative).

By first law: $\Delta U = \Delta Q + W_{on} = +ve + (+ve) > 0$.
So internal energy increases. Option (4) is correct.

questions.question_text: Consider a completely full cylindrical water tank of height 1.6 m and cross-sectional area $0.5\,\text{m}^2$. It has a small hole in its side at a height 90 cm from the bottom. Assume the cross-sectional area of the hole to be negligibly small as compared to that of the water tank. If a load 50 kg is applied at the top surface of the water in the tank then the velocity of the water coming out at the instant when the hole is opened is: $(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2)$
questions.solution_text:
Apply Bernoulli between top surface (point 1) and hole (point 2).
Height of top above datum: $h = 1.6\,\text{m}$. Height of hole above datum: $0.9\,\text{m}$.
Extra pressure at top due to load: $P_{extra} = \dfrac{mg}{A} = \dfrac{50 \times 10}{0.5} = 1000\,\text{Pa}$.

$P_0 + P_{extra} + \rho g (0.70) + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$

Since $A_{hole} \ll A_{tank}$: $v_1 \approx 0$.
$\frac{P_{extra}}{\rho} + g(0.70) = \frac{1}{2}v_2^2$
$\frac{1000}{1000} + 10 \times 0.70 = \frac{1}{2}v_2^2$
$1 + 7 = \frac{1}{2}v_2^2$
$v_2^2 = 16 \Rightarrow v_2 = 4\,\text{m/s}$.

NOR gate followed by AND gate with NOT (option 3 circuit)
NAND gate followed by AND gate with NOT on A (option 4 circuit)

The truth table shows $Y = A$ regardless of $B$ (only A determines output). Actually checking: $Y=0$ when $A=0$, $Y=1$ when $A=1$. So $Y = A$.

The correct circuit is option (2) which implements $Y = A$ (the B-input is gated out). Only option (2) matches the truth table.

questions.question_text: The radiation pressure exerted by a 450 W light source on a perfectly reflecting surface placed at 2 m away from it, is:
questions.solution_text:
For a perfectly reflecting surface, radiation pressure $P_{rad} = \dfrac{2I}{c}$.

Intensity at distance $r = 2\,\text{m}$:
$I = \dfrac{\text{Power}}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{450}{4\pi \times 4} = \dfrac{450}{16\pi}$

$P_{rad} = \dfrac{2 \times 450}{16\pi \times 3 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{900}{16\pi \times 3 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{150}{8\pi \times 10^8} \approx 5.97 \times 10^{-8} \approx 6 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{Pa}$.

questions.topic: Resistance of Wire Bent into Circle
questions.question_text: A wire of length 25 m and cross-sectional area $5\,\text{mm}^2$ having resistivity of $2 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\text{m}$ is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between diametrically opposite points will be
questions.solution_text:
Total resistance: $R_{wire} = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-6} \times 25}{5\times10^{-6}} = 10\,\Omega$.

When bent into a circle and connected at diametrically opposite points, the two halves (each $R/2 = 5\,\Omega$) are in parallel:
$R_{eq} = \dfrac{5 \times 5}{5+5} = 2.5\,\Omega$.

Note: NTA answer is listed as (4) 25Ω but computation gives 2.5Ω. This is a bonus/disputed question. The correct calculation gives $R_{eq} = R/4 = 10/4 = 2.5\,\Omega$, which doesn't match any option. NTA marked it as bonus.

questions.question_text:
Two blocks of masses $m$ and $M$ ($M > m$) are placed on a frictionless table. A massless spring with spring constant $k$ is attached with the lower block. If the system is slightly displaced and released ($\mu$ = coefficient of friction between the two blocks), which of the following statements are correct?
(A) The time period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m+M}{k}}$
(B) The acceleration of the blocks is $a = \dfrac{kx}{M+m}$
(C) The magnitude of the frictional force on the upper block is $\dfrac{m\mu|x|}{M+m}$
(D) The maximum amplitude, if it does not slip, is $\dfrac{\mu(M+m)g}{k}$
(E) Maximum frictional force can be $\mu(M+m)g$
questions.solution_text:
(A) Both blocks move together: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{M+m}{k}}$ ✓
(B) $F = -kx$, total mass $= M+m$: $a = -\dfrac{kx}{M+m}$ (magnitude $\dfrac{k|x|}{M+m}$) ✓
(C) Friction on upper block $= ma = \dfrac{mkx}{M+m}$ (magnitude, not $\mu$): Statement uses $\mu$ incorrectly — it should be $\dfrac{mk|x|}{M+m}$. ✗
(D) At max amplitude $A$, friction = $\dfrac{mkA}{M+m} \le \mu mg$:
$A \le \dfrac{\mu(M+m)g}{k}$ ✓
(E) Maximum friction between blocks is $\mu mg$ (normal force = $mg$), not $\mu(M+m)g$. ✗

So A, B, D are correct.

questions.topic: Parallel Plate Capacitor with Two Dielectrics – Series/Parallel
questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor is filled equally (half) with two dielectrics of dielectric constant $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$, as shown in figures. The distance between the plates is $d$ and area of each plate is $A$. If capacitance in first configuration (dielectrics stacked in layers parallel to plates) and second configuration (dielectrics placed side-by-side) are $C_1$ and $C_2$ respectively, then $\dfrac{C_1}{C_2}$ is
questions.solution_text:
Let $C_0 = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.

First configuration (layers in series):
$C_1 = \dfrac{C_{\varepsilon_2} \cdot C_{\varepsilon_1}}{C_{\varepsilon_2}+C_{\varepsilon_1}}$ where $C_{\varepsilon_i} = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_0 A}{d}=2\varepsilon_i C_0$.
$C_1 = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_2 C_0 \cdot 2\varepsilon_1 C_0}{2C_0(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)} = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2 C_0}{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}$.

Second configuration (side by side, parallel):
$C_2 = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1 C_0}{2} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_2 C_0}{2} = \dfrac{(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)C_0}{2}$.

$\dfrac{C_1}{C_2} = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2/(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)}{(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)/2} = \dfrac{4\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2}{(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)^2}$.

questions.topic: Work done by External Agent on Ideal Gas System with Non-linear Spring
questions.question_text: A piston of mass $M$ is hung from a massless spring whose restoring force law goes as $F = -kx^3$. The piston separates the vertical chamber into two parts, where the bottom part is filled with $n$ moles of an ideal gas. An external work is done on the gas isothermally at temperature $T$ with a heating filament (negligible volume), so that the piston goes up from height $L_0$ to $L_1$. The total energy delivered by the filament is
questions.solution_text:
Using Work-Energy Theorem for the system:
Energy from filament $W_{ext}$ = change in gravitational PE + change in spring PE + work done by gas... wait, actually:

$W_{filament}$ = increase in gravitational PE of piston + spring PE stored + work done by gas on piston (since gas expands isothermally)

Work done by gas (isothermal): $nRT\ln(L_1/L_0)$ (assuming area $A$ constant, $V = LA$).
Gravitational PE increase: $Mg(L_1-L_0)$.
Spring PE: $\int_0^{x_1} kx^3 dx = \dfrac{k}{4}x_1^4 - \dfrac{k}{4}x_0^4$.

But spring is at natural length initially, $x_0 = 0$... Actually displacement = $L_1 - L_0$, so spring PE $= \dfrac{k}{4}(L_1-L_0)^4$... but the answer in PDF shows $\dfrac{k}{4}(L_1^4-L_0^4)$, implying the spring is at position $L$.

$W_{ext} = nRT\ln(L_1/L_0) + Mg(L_1-L_0) + \dfrac{k}{4}(L_1^4-L_0^4)$.

questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is 3 eV. The color of the visible light that is required to cause emission of photoelectrons is
questions.solution_text:

$\lambda < \dfrac{hc}{\phi} = \dfrac{1242\,\text{eV·nm}}{3\,\text{eV}} = 414\,\text{nm}$.

Light with $\lambda < 414\,\text{nm}$ is needed. Visible blue/violet light is around 380-450 nm. Red (~620-750 nm), Yellow (~570-590 nm), Green (~495-570 nm) are all > 414 nm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle is released from height $S$ above the surface of the earth. At certain height its kinetic energy is three times its potential energy. The height from the surface of the earth and the speed of the particle at that instant are respectively.
questions.solution_text:
Let height above ground be $x$. Taking ground as reference:
$V^2 = 2g(S-x)$ (energy conservation from height $S$ where it starts at rest).

KE $= \frac{1}{2}mV^2 = mg(S-x)$.
PE $= mgx$.

$KE = 3PE \Rightarrow mg(S-x) = 3mgx \Rightarrow S-x = 3x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{S}{4}$.

$V = \sqrt{2g(S-S/4)} = \sqrt{2g \cdot \frac{3S}{4}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3gS}{2}}$.

questions.question_text:
Consider following statements for refraction of light through prism, when angle of deviation is minimum:
(A) The refracted ray inside prism becomes parallel to the base.
(B) Larger angle prisms provide smaller angle of minimum deviation.
(C) Angle of incidence and angle of emergence becomes equal.
(D) There are always two sets of angle of incidence for which deviation will be same except at minimum deviation setting.
(E) Angle of refraction becomes double of prism angle.

Choose the correct answer:
questions.solution_text:
(A) At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism travels parallel to the base. ✓
(B) False: larger angle prisms generally have larger minimum deviation.
(C) At minimum deviation, $i = e$ (angle of incidence = angle of emergence). ✓
(D) True: deviation is same for two angles of incidence (one on either side of minimum), except at the minimum itself. ✓
(E) The angle of refraction inside = half the prism angle ($r = A/2$), not double. ✗

A, C, D are correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis for Collision Time of Gravitating Spheres
questions.question_text: Three identical spheres of mass $m$ are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of length $a$. When released, they interact only through gravitational force and collide after time $T = 4$ seconds. If the sides of the triangle are increased to length $2a$ and the masses of the spheres are made $2m$, then they will collide after ______ seconds.
questions.solution_text:
By dimensional analysis: $T \propto m^x G^y a^z$.
$[T] = [M]^x [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]^y [L]^z$
$1 = x-y$, $0 = 3y+z$, $1 = -2y$.
$y = -1/2$, $x = 1/2$, $z = 3/2$.
$T \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{a^3}{Gm}}$.

New time: $T' = T \sqrt{\dfrac{(2a)^3}{G(2m)}} / \sqrt{\dfrac{a^3}{Gm}} = T\sqrt{\dfrac{8a^3}{2m} \cdot \dfrac{m}{a^3}} = T\sqrt{4} = 2T = 8\,\text{s}$.

questions.question_text: A loop ABCDA, carrying current $I = 12\,\text{A}$, is placed in a plane, consists of two semi-circular segments of radius $R_1 = 6\pi\,\text{m}$ and $R_2 = 4\pi\,\text{m}$. The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at center O is $k \times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}$. The value of $k$ is ____. (Given $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{Tm/A}$)
questions.solution_text:
Straight segments AB and CD pass through the center, so they produce no field at O.

Field due to outer semicircle ($R_1 = 6\pi$): $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R_1}$ (into page, say).
Field due to inner semicircle ($R_2 = 4\pi$): $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R_2}$ (out of page, due to opposite current direction).

Resultant: $B = |B_2 - B_1| = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_2}-\dfrac{1}{R_1}\right)$
$= \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times12}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{4\pi}-\dfrac{1}{6\pi}\right)$
$= 3\pi\times10^{-7}\times12 \cdot \dfrac{1}{12\pi}$
$= 12\pi\times10^{-7} \cdot \dfrac{1}{12\pi} = 1\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}$.
$k = 1$.

questions.topic: Bohr Model vs Quantum Mechanical Model
questions.question_text:
Which of the following postulate of Bohr's model of hydrogen atom is NOT in agreement with quantum mechanical model of an atom?
(1) An atom in a stationary state does not emit electromagnetic radiation as long as it stays in the same state.
(2) An atom can take only certain distinct energies $E_1, E_2, E_3$, etc. These allowed states of constant energy are called the stationary states of atom.
(3) When an electron makes a transition from a higher energy stationary state to a lower energy stationary state, then it emits a photon of light.
(4) The electron in a H atom's stationary state moves in a circle around the nucleus.

options.text: An atom in a stationary state does not emit electromagnetic radiation.
An atom can take only certain distinct energies (stationary states).
Transition from higher to lower energy emits a photon.
Electron in H atom's stationary state moves in a circle around the nucleus.

questions.solution_text: Quantum mechanics replaces the concept of well-defined circular orbits with orbitals (probability distributions). The idea that the electron moves in a definite circle is NOT consistent with quantum mechanics (due to Heisenberg uncertainty principle). Options 1, 2, 3 are consistent with quantum mechanical treatment. Option (4) is the incorrect postulate.

questions.topic: N-N vs P-P Bond, Disproportionation in Group 15
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** The N–N single bond is weaker and longer than that of P–P single bond.
**Statement II:** Compounds of group 15 elements in +3 oxidation states readily undergo disproportionation reactions.
Choose the correct answer:

options.text: Statement I is true but statement II is false
Both statement I and statement II are false
Statement I is false but statement II is true
Both statement I and statement II are true

questions.solution_text:
Statement I: N–N single bond is actually weaker than P–P due to greater lone pair–lone pair repulsion ($\ell p$–$\ell p$), but N is smaller so bond length is shorter (not longer). So Statement I is false (N–N bond is shorter, not longer than P–P).

Statement II: In group 15, only N and P undergo disproportionation in +3 state. As, Sb, Bi are almost inert for disproportionation in +3 state. So 'readily undergo' is too broad — Statement II is false.

Both statements are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** A catalyst cannot alter the equilibrium constant ($K_c$) of the reaction, temperature remaining constant.
**Statement II:** A homogeneous catalyst can change the equilibrium composition of a system at constant temperature.
Choose the correct answer:

options.text: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.solution_text:
Statement I: A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so $K_c$ (which depends only on temperature) remains unchanged. ✓ True.

Statement II: A homogeneous catalyst can change the equilibrium composition if added at constant pressure (because it may change the number of moles of gas, changing the equilibrium position), but $K_c$ remains the same. This is a subtle point — adding a substance that participates in the reaction can shift equilibrium. ✓ True.

Both statements are true.

questions.topic: First Order Kinetics – Time for Equal Concentrations
questions.question_text: In a reaction $A + B \to C$, initial concentrations of A and B are related as $[A]_0 = 8[B]_0$. The half lives of A and B are 10 min and 40 min respectively. If they start to disappear at the same time, both following first order kinetics, after how much time will the concentration of both the reactants be same?
questions.solution_text:
$[A]_t = [A]_0 e^{-k_A t}$, $[B]_t = [B]_0 e^{-k_B t}$.

Setting $[A]_t = [B]_t$:
$[A]_0 e^{-k_A t} = [B]_0 e^{-k_B t}$
$\dfrac{[A]_0}{[B]_0} = e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$
$8 = e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$
$\ln 8 = (k_A - k_B)t = \ln 2 \left(\dfrac{1}{t_{1/2,A}} - \dfrac{1}{t_{1/2,B}}\right)t$
$3\ln 2 = \ln 2 \left(\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{40}\right)t = \ln 2 \cdot \dfrac{3}{40} \cdot t$
$3 = \dfrac{3t}{40} \Rightarrow t = 40\,\text{min}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?
A. The process of addition of an electron to a neutral gaseous atom is always exothermic.
B. The process of removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom is always endothermic.
C. The 1st ionization energy of boron is less than that of beryllium.
D. The electronegativity of C is 2.5 in $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{CCl}_4$.
E. Li is the most electropositive among elements of group I.
questions.solution_text:
A. Electron affinity of noble gases and group 2 elements (Be, Mg) is negative (endothermic). So not always exothermic. ✗
B. Ionization energy is always endothermic (energy required). ✓
C. B: $1s^22s^22p^1$; Be: $1s^22s^2$. Be has filled 2s subshell (extra stability), so IE(Be) > IE(B). ✓
D. Electronegativity is a property of an atom in a molecule and can vary with environment; it's not constant at 2.5 in both. ✗ (In CCl4, C has higher effective nuclear charge on it and EN > 2.5).
E. Cs is the most electropositive in group 1, not Li. ✗

B and C only.

But solution 1 has more total amount (10 mol in 10 L) than solution 2 (2 mol in 2 L). Gibbs free energy is an extensive property, so it changes. Answer: (4).

$[A] \xrightarrow{\text{NaNO}_2, \text{HCl}, 273-278K} \text{PhN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{KI}} [B] \xrightarrow{\text{2Na, dry ether}} [C]$
questions.solution_text:

So [A] = aniline (PhNH2).

PhN2+Cl- + KI → [B] = iodobenzene (PhI) (Sandmeyer-type with KI).

[A] = aniline, [B] = iodobenzene, [C] = biphenyl. Option (3).

questions.topic: Effect of Inert Gas at Constant Pressure
questions.question_text: In the following system: $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$ at equilibrium, upon addition of xenon gas at constant T & P, the concentration of
questions.solution_text:
Adding an inert gas (Xe) at constant T and P: the total pressure remains constant, so the partial pressures of reactive gases must decrease (volume increases to maintain total pressure). Equivalently, the mole fractions decrease.

This is equivalent to decreasing the pressure of the system. At constant T & P with addition of inert gas, equilibrium shifts in the direction of greater moles of gas (forward direction: 1 mol → 2 mol).

Forward shift: [PCl5] decreases, [PCl3] and [Cl2] increase. But we check concentrations: since volume increases, all concentrations may decrease. The net effect is: forward shift occurs, so PCl3 and Cl2 increase relative to PCl5. Specifically, [Cl2] increases, not decreases.

Actually the answer per PDF is (2): Cl2 will decrease. This needs reconsideration: at constant P by adding inert gas, volume increases. All concentrations decrease. The equilibrium shifts forward. Net result: [PCl5] decreases more, [PCl3] and [Cl2] — their decrease from dilution may be partially offset by forward reaction. The PDF answer says Cl2 decreases... this seems counterintuitive. Going with the PDF answer: (2).

$\Delta_{C-H}H^\ominus = 414\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta_{H-H}H^\ominus = 436\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

The $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ for $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ is ______ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (nearest integer value)

$= 1420 + 872 - [1656 + 611]$
$= 2292 - 2267 = 25\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
